sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A book that looks like the team that made it
sections.para: Before designing the book of the talk I asked for research: what Markua and print on demand allow, what the best visual books do, and what the research on learning says about pictures and words. The answer is a plan an agent team can carry out by machine.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines from the signal to the plan
sections.para: The book must look like its workflow; the page allows more than it seems; the research favours words and pictures together; the best books do it by hand; agents can do it by machine; animations become filmstrips; and ten things the book will do.

sections.label: Why a book has to look like its workflow
sections.line: Why the look is the signal
sections.para: The talk looked like it was made by an agent team, and that was part of the argument. A book made by agents that looks like any other contradicts its message, and a book is a teaching aid, so the starting point is evidence, not convention.

sections.label: What the page allows
sections.line: What Markua and print on demand allow
sections.para: Markua sizes, floats and bleeds images, numbers captions, keeps SVG and Mermaid as text and has seven typed boxes; it has no raw HTML, no text on both sides of an image, and discourages page breaks. Print asks for 300 DPI and all-or-nothing bleed, and colour costs two to five times black ink per page.

sections.label: What the best visual books do
sections.line: What the best visual books do
sections.para: Tufte's small multiples, Head First's words on pictures, Wardley's one map grammar, Brown's one notation, Evans's one idea per page, Munroe's word list, McCloud's panels, Fowler's duplex book, Nystrom's registration marks and tested code, and Quantum Country's questions: by hand, what a pipeline does by default.

sections.label: What the learning research says
sections.para: Mayer's experiments favour words with pictures (1.39), placed together (1.09), without decoration (0.97), in segments, with the concepts named first and a conversational voice; upper bounds from short lessons. Dual coding is not learning styles, and practice testing and spacing are rated most useful.

sections.label: Where the industry is
sections.para: Leanpub sells AI tools for alt text and indexes; Amazon capped self-publishers at three titles a day; the useful trend is books that version like software, built from repositories, which RC1 already is.

sections.label: What an agent team adds
sections.para: Every figure a run with a spec, as in the talk's 25 ruv.sgit runs; a change made in minutes on request; a visual grammar enforced by a checker; animations as stills at named seconds; and reviews turned into decisions, as in RC1's companion.

sections.label: The plan for the book
sections.line: Ten things the book will do
sections.para: A cast of concepts up front, one map grammar, filmstrips with links to the moving version, words on the drawing, call-outs as Markua boxes, greyscale first, no decoration, questions asked again later, every number with its id, and every figure a spec. All of it shared.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: Research by an agent in one session, with Tufte's site blocked and Head First paraphrased; Mayer's effect sizes are upper bounds; the Leanpub picks are editorial; the costs change; the plan is untested.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.para: The Markua specification, Leanpub's update and help, KDP's help pages, Mayer's chapter abstracts, Weinstein and colleagues and Dunlosky and colleagues, the books' own pages, the Authors Guild, and the talk's and the book's repositories.
